description.p: rPGP is an OpenPGP certificate manager in the spirit of KDE's Kleopatra: a window that lists your certificates and lets you generate, import, export, certify, sign, encrypt, decrypt and verify without touching a command line.

It keeps two questions apart that are easy to confuse and dangerous to mix up: whether a certificate is internally valid, and whether the name on it belongs to the person you think. The first is arithmetic; the second is the web of trust, computed from the certifications in your own store.

ul.li: Generate keys to RFC 9580 or RFC 4880, with a passphrase and a pre-made revocation certificate
Sign, encrypt, decrypt and verify files, or text in a built-in notepad
Encrypt to certificates, to a password, or to both at once
Certify identities, mark trusted introducers, and see what authenticates a key
Revoke keys, user IDs and subkeys, with the consequences spelled out
Look up and publish keys over WKD and HKPS
Use keys held on a smartcard through gpg-agent, so the secret never leaves the card

description.p: Written in Rust throughout, using Sequoia for OpenPGP and Slint for the interface. No webview, no Qt, and it never shells out to gpg.

description.p: A way to read signatures from certificates too old for the standard policy, and fixes to what the verification banner manages to say.

ul.li: Keys certified before about 2010 sign themselves with SHA-1, so rPGP found no valid identity and no valid subkey on them and showed the whole certificate as unusable — accurate, and no help to someone trying to check a signature a project still publishes. Such a certificate now offers to accept SHA-1 from that one certificate

Accepting it widens what can be checked and nothing else. The certificate still cannot be authenticated through the web of trust, act as a trust root, vouch for another key, or be encrypted to, and every other certificate is judged exactly as strictly as before in the same operation

What comes back is not a guarantee, and says so. SHA-1 collisions are practical, so a signature that checks out shows the signer's key was involved rather than that its holder approved the document. The result leads with that, ahead of the identity verdict, and the signature is marked SHA-1 wherever it is listed
The offer appears only where it would help — where SHA-1 is the reason the certificate is unusable, not on one that is broken some other way

The reason a verification failed could be cut off in the decrypt and verify banner, sliced along the top and bottom of a box built for a single line. The longer the failure, the less of it survived, which is backwards for the message that most needs reading
That banner counted every wrapped line as one, so a verdict running to three lines was drawn outside its coloured box entirely. It is now sized to the text it actually draws
A certificate list that loads while part of the store cannot be read now names the part that failed, rather than leaving a badge missing with no explanation

description.p: A Windows build, and fixes from a second review of the whole tree plus the first end-to-end testing on each platform.

ul.li: rPGP now runs on Windows
Signing text that ended without a proper line ending produced a signature rPGP itself then called invalid. Text copied from a Windows application and trimmed of its last blank line did exactly that

A certificate revoked twice showed the most recent reason rather than the most serious, so a later "no longer used" could hide "the secret key may be compromised" — which anyone holding the stolen key could arrange
Certifying an identity its owner had revoked is now refused. A revoked address is one the holder has disowned, and often one the provider has since given to somebody else
The expiry of a key imported from GnuPG could not be changed at all. Keys with an authentication subkey, which is what GnuPG makes, failed the whole operation
A message that was signed but never encrypted was reported as decrypted, telling the reader that something which crossed the network in clear had arrived confidentially
Importing a file that held part of a key you already had could discard the material you held. The two are now merged
A certification is attributed only after it verifies, so a packet naming your key without being signed by it can no longer appear in the list as yours
Verified badges belong to an identity rather than to the whole certificate, so an unauthenticated name on a key can no longer inherit another identity's verdict
A screen reader can now see which recipients are selected, and every dropdown says what it is for
Toolbar buttons no longer overlap when the window is narrow
A failure to open the certificate store now says so, instead of the app starting and vanishing without a word
An oversized or padded message is refused rather than allowed to exhaust memory or CPU

description.p: Fixes found by a security and optimization review of the whole tree.

ul.li: Decrypting a file could destroy an unrelated file that happened to sit at the name used for the temporary output

A secret key that arrived by import silently became a web-of-trust root, so an imported key could make identities it had certified read as verified. Keys you generate are still roots; an imported one can be made one from its details pane
Certifying an identity could be silently prevented by a planted revocation packet that named your key without being signed by it
Publishing reported success when the confirmation-mail request had failed, leaving an address the keyserver would never serve
Keyserver lookups no longer follow redirects to private addresses
The interface font is bundled, so the app looks the same however it is installed
Reloading a large keyring is roughly twice as fast
